classification_signals: Research Methodology: Approach to theoretical analysis: arguing theoretical points (Page 1)
The research explains the concept of sensory perception of architectural spaces as a multi-sensory tool for experiencing and interpreting the environment (Page 1)
A discussion of multisensory design ideas for establishing a healthy environment for visually impaired students, as well as the necessity of multisensory architecture. (Page 1)
The paper synthesizes existing knowledge and design principles to propose standards, rather than presenting new empirical data or statistical analyses.
title: The impact of sensory perception on interior architecture standards for visually impaired and blind students in educational facilities

findings.antecedent: Multisensory architectural design (texture, sound, heat, aroma)
findings.consequent: Visually impaired persons' ability to define spaces and functions, and better grasp their environment
findings.quote: Architects use employ texture, sound, heat, and aroma to define spaces and functions.

findings.antecedent: Disturbance of one sense (e.g., vision)
findings.consequent: Adaptability to the environment
findings.source: Sensory perception and its effect on creating criteria for blind interior design
findings.quote: When one of the senses is disturbed, the rest of the senses are affected, resulting in low adaptability to the environment

findings.antecedent: Incorporating many senses into building design and creating a multisensory constructed environment
findings.consequent: Interactive (dynamic) architecture, allowing senses to feel connected while thinking independently
findings.source: Sensory perception and its effect on creating criteria for blind interior design
findings.quote: By incorporating many senses into building design and creating a multisensory constructed environment... we can design spaces for the blind and create an interactive (dynamic) architecture

findings.antecedent: Design that communicates through remaining functional senses (acoustic, tactile, smell architecture)
findings.consequent: Visually impaired people's benefit from the design
findings.source: Sensory perception and its effect on creating criteria for blind interior design
findings.quote: According to sensory architecture research, visually impaired people benefit from a design that communicates with them through their remaining functional senses.

findings.antecedent: Auditory, tactile, and olfactory clues
findings.consequent: Blind person's mental picture of the voyage (cognitive map) and spatial perceptions
findings.source: Sensory perception and its effect on creating criteria for blind interior design
findings.quote: A blind person's spatial perceptions are formed through the use of a cognitive map comprised of routes and landmarks... physically defined by auditory, tactile, and olfactory clues.

findings.antecedent: Loss or disruption of visual sense
findings.consequent: Struggle to engage with surroundings
findings.source: Sensory perception and its effect on creating criteria for blind interior design
findings.quote: When this sense is lost or disrupted, the person struggles to engage with his surroundings.

findings.antecedent: Variety of flooring materials (textural contrast)
findings.consequent: Simplicity to differentiate moving pathways
findings.quote: Use a variety of flooring materials to provide textural contrast, making it simpler to differentiate moving pathways from one spot to another.

findings.antecedent: Texture in walls aligned to movement pathways
findings.consequent: Understanding directional spaces
findings.quote: Understanding directional spaces by the use of texture in walls that may be aligned to internal and exterior movement pathways.

findings.antecedent: Dotted or longitudinal track on movement routes (contrasting materials)
findings.consequent: Ease of moving down a straight path for blind users with a stick
findings.quote: It's a dotted or longitudinal track that makes moving down a straight path easier.

findings.antecedent: Different sounds for each interior space (e.g., sound of water) and heating units providing specific heat sources
findings.consequent: Blind or visually impaired users' ability to perceive a specific path and sense of emptiness
findings.quote: by using different sounds for each space, such as the sound of water, and heating units can be used to provide a specific path for the blind or visually impaired to feel the heat source

findings.antecedent: Handrail with tactile braille text and other tactile pathways
findings.consequent: Vision-impaired youngsters' navigation of the site
findings.quote: The use of a handrail with tactile braille text as well as other forms of tactile pathways across the site will substantially assist vision-impaired youngsters in navigating the site.

findings.antecedent: Sound effects added to long paths in educational facilities
findings.consequent: Feeling disoriented for blind children
findings.quote: Adding sound effects to the long Paths to avoid feeling disoriented in a blind children's educational facility.

findings.antecedent: Sound produced by stick colliding with protrusions and sensations experienced
findings.consequent: Route direction for blind users
findings.quote: The sound produced by the stick colliding with the protrusions, as well as the sensations it experiences, provide some route direction.

findings.antecedent: Sense of smell (e.g., flowers and trees)
findings.consequent: Children's ability to identify directions or places at crossroads or along lengthy paths
findings.quote: Space With the usage of effects the sense of smell in children is beneficial to identify directions or places at crossroads or along lengthy Paths.

findings.antecedent: Classroom spaces bigger than typical with divisions for individual/small group work
findings.consequent: Smoother circulation, inspiring place to work, negotiate, and cooperate for peers
findings.quote: The most important aspect of classroom spaces is that they are bigger than typical to allow for smoother circulation inside specifically equipped instructional rooms

findings.antecedent: ICT equipment (network computer workstations, interactive writing board with Braille writing capability)
findings.consequent: Students with visual disabilities' ability to get the most out of the learning process
findings.quote: Having ICT equipment in the classroom... allows students with visual disabilities to get the most out of the learning process

findings.antecedent: Different smells (e.g., fire, smoke, gas leakage)
findings.consequent: Students' ability to recognize potential harm from daily life
findings.quote: using different smells to teach students about the smell of potential harm such as fire, smoke, gas leakage, etc.

findings.antecedent: Sound recordings of various environments
findings.consequent: Students' perception of the world
findings.quote: Used sound recordings of the various environment to stimulate students' perception of the world.

findings.antecedent: Lighting designed to exercise and stimulate visibility
findings.consequent: Low-vision children's visibility
findings.quote: The lighting is designed to exercise and stimulate visibility in low-vision children.

findings.antecedent: Smooth furniture surfaces free of sharp edges or bumps
findings.consequent: Safety for blind and visually impaired children
findings.quote: Furniture surfaces for blind and visually impaired children should be smooth and free of sharp edges.

findings.antecedent: Noise and gleaming surfaces
findings.consequent: Vision for blind and visually impaired children
findings.quote: Noise and gleaming surfaces might limit vision and should be avoided.

findings.antecedent: Floors that are damp or slippery, or have wide gaps between units, or are made of sand, asphalt, or gravel (outdoor)
findings.consequent: Safety and mobility for blind and visually impaired users (with stick or wheelchair)
findings.quote: Floors should not be damp or slippery... gaps between the units should not be so wide that they obstruct the stick or wheelchair... Sand, asphalt, and gravel flooring should not be utilized in outdoor areas because they obstruct the movement of strollers and wheelchairs.

findings.antecedent: More than one type of flooring
findings.consequent: Blind users' ability to recognize different spaces and determine direction
findings.quote: It is normally preferable to use more than one type of flooring to help the blind in recognizing the different spaces and determining the direction of the various places.

findings.antecedent: Contrasting colors on the floor (e.g., dark squares)
findings.consequent: Navigation for people with limited vision
findings.quote: Using contrasting colours on the floor to help with navigation: People with limited vision can benefit from dark squares indicating the path down the main driveway

findings.antecedent: Straight paths and clear, sharp angles
findings.consequent: Ease of navigation within a space
findings.quote: Steer the path as straight as possible. Straight paths and clear and sharp angles can help people navigate the path within your space more easily.

findings.antecedent: Hand support on both sides of walls (85-95 cm height, 40-50mm diameter cushions)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding and support for visually impaired users
findings.quote: Equipping the walls with hand support on both sides of the walls at a height of between 85 cm and 95 cm, and preferably in the cushions should be circular in diameter between 40mm and 50mm.

findings.antecedent: Contrasting colors or fabric, boundaries, and conspicuous indications on stairs
findings.consequent: Clarity of stairs for visual impairment
findings.quote: To make stairs clearer for visual impairment by using the senses of touch and visuals around the stairs we can use contrasting colours or fabric, boundaries, and conspicuous indications.

findings.antecedent: Braille on walls and divided materials on flooring
findings.consequent: Use of texture for visually impaired users
findings.quote: Make use of texture by writing Braille on the walls and dividing the materials on the flooring.

findings.antecedent: Contrasting colour scheme
findings.consequent: Pupils' ability to guide themselves in corridors and playgrounds
findings.quote: A contrasting colour scheme can be regarded as a core issue in visually impaired meddlers. Colours can play a key role in helping pupils guide themselves both in the corridor and on the playground.

findings.antecedent: Bright colors in large spaces or crowded patterns
findings.consequent: Visual comfort and influence
findings.quote: Bright colours in large spaces or crowded patterns can build a strong influence better to be avoided.

findings.antecedent: Dim pastel colours
findings.consequent: Soothing effect
findings.quote: Dim pastel colours can be soothing.

findings.antecedent: Glare, shadows, and other visual interference from lighting
findings.consequent: Visual conflicts and sensitivity for visually impaired students
findings.quote: Design lighting should avoid glare, shadows, and any other interference that can cause visual conflicts, most students with visual impairment are particularly sensitive to glare from direct or reflected sunlight.

findings.antecedent: Dark curtains (controlling sunlight/daylight levels)
findings.consequent: Comfort and improved visibility
findings.quote: Use dark curtains to control sunlight or daylight levels for added comfort and improved visibility.

findings.antecedent: LED lamp (simulating daylight, homogeneous lighting, low-glare, no unwanted flash/noise)
findings.consequent: Higher efficiency and longer life, preferred lighting for visually impaired
findings.quote: preferred use an LED lamp that simulates daylight, giving homogeneous lighting, higher efficiency, and longer life.

findings.antecedent: Room acoustics and isolation of sound (between rooms and external noise)
findings.consequent: Visually impaired children's access to learning (relying on hearing)
findings.quote: Providing room acoustics and isolating sound between rooms and external noise improves their access to learning.

findings.antecedent: Double glass
findings.consequent: Volume noise sound reduction
findings.quote: The use of double glass should provide the required volume noise sound reduction.

findings.antecedent: Absorbent surfaces in the ceiling
findings.consequent: Optimal sound quality
findings.quote: Use absorbent surfaces for optimal sound quality in the ceiling.

findings.antecedent: Audio signals in critical places (e.g., alarm/countdown at intersection)
findings.consequent: Safety for blind users when crossing
findings.quote: Use audio signals in critical places. Adding an alarm or countdown to an intersection, for example, can make the crossing safer by alerting the blind user when the crossing is safe.

findings.antecedent: Design that compensates for the sense of sight in other senses (multisensory stimulation)
findings.consequent: Visually impaired users' ability to recognize and deal with different internal spaces
findings.quote: The design idea is to compensate for the sense of sight in the other senses. Multisensory stimulation: Providing a variety of contacts, sounds, and odours to restore life to the inner void can help the visually impaired recognize and deal with different internal spaces

findings.antecedent: One axis of movement linked to slanted movement with horizontal/flat surfaces on right and tilted/curved surfaces on left
findings.consequent: Confirmation of direction and ease of recognizing the vacuum (space)
findings.quote: one axis of movement... was linked to a slanted movement, the right side of which represents horizontal and flat surfaces, and the left side has tilted and curved surfaces, thus confirming the direction and making it easier to recognize the vacuum.

findings.antecedent: Wood as a material (distinguishing space by touch, absorbing sound, distinctive smell)
findings.consequent: Spatial identification, auditory comfort, and reduced fear for users
findings.quote: Wood is used to distinguish the space using the sense of touch... Wood absorbs sound... Wood has a distinctive smell that makes users of the vacuum distinguish it without fear.

findings.antecedent: Design of interior spaces considering needs of all people (including vision difficulties)
findings.consequent: Accessibility and usability for all categories of people
findings.quote: When designing different interior spaces, the needs of all people who will use them, including those with vision difficulties, must be taken into account

findings.antecedent: Appropriate designs in buildings and outdoor spaces (accommodating challenges of visually impaired)
findings.consequent: Creation of spaces that accommodate everyone who needs to use them
findings.quote: By understanding the challenges faced by the visually impaired, and implementing appropriate designs in buildings and outdoor spaces to accommodate them can create spaces that accommodate everyone who needs to use them.

findings.antecedent: Simplified movement paths and easy-to-use entrances/vertical communication means
findings.consequent: Facilitation of mental image, access to all roles of the building, and use of emergency exits for visually impaired
findings.quote: Simplifying the movement paths to facilitate the mental image and stay away from different levels on the floors must be the Paths leading to the emergency exits are easy to use

limitations: Existing educational spaces for people with special needs are lacking, leading to restriction and dependence for visually impaired individuals (Abstract, Page 1).
Visually impaired persons live in constrained and limited surroundings, requiring guiding services and support to adapt to the sighted world and overcome unpleasant reactions (Page 1).
minimum_safe_summary: This theoretical paper argues for the critical role of multisensory perception in designing interior architecture standards for visually impaired and blind students in educational facilities. It highlights that architecture should be a multisensory art, compensating for visual impairment by engaging other senses like touch, hearing, and smell. Key findings include the importance of tactile and auditory cues for wayfinding and spatial understanding, the need for contrasting materials and colors for navigation and safety, and the design of classrooms and movement paths to support learning and independence. The paper emphasizes Universal Design principles to create accessible and comfortable environments. A primary limitation identified is the current lack of qualified educational spaces for visually impaired individuals, leading to their restriction and dependence.
